en: The Secret Dhāraṇī Method for the Threefold Siddhi: Breaking Through Hell, Transforming Karmic Obstructions, and Escaping the Triple World,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of Central India by Imperial Decree.

The ritual methods of Yoga number in the thousands; here, a brief portion is described: when the mouth opens and the tongue is raised, the palace of the Dharma-realm trembles. The Tathāgata of the Lotus Treasury World emerges from meditative absorption, immediately shattering the hells, transforming karmic obstructions, and delivering beings from the three realms.
It should be known that when the characters are inscribed according to the Dharma, and the sovereign wears them upon his crown and headgear, the myriad nations will enjoy purity and tranquility;
when the military governors and regional inspectors inscribe the mantras upon their banners and flags, the four quarters will be peaceful and still.

When a Prefectural Governor employs this to suppress and pacify [the region], if one inscribes characters upon a war drum and strikes it with great solemnity, its sound will be heard from afar. Malevolent vapors will be cleared away as they blaze intensely over a thousand *li*, the crops will receive abundant moisture, and the people will be free from calamities and epidemics. The deities of the earth will respond so that the winds are calm and the rains timely; by reciting mantras and performing empowerments (*adhitiṣṭhati*) while inscribing [mantras] upon a battle drum, enemy armies will surrender of their own accord, not a single person being harmed—this is called the "Vajra Drum."
I prostrate to Vairocana Buddha, whose pure eyes bloom like lotuses;
The Tamer of the Three Realms, Teacher of Gods and Humans, The Savior of the World through the Great Bodhicitta.
Through the empowerment of the profound and wondrous mantras, They flow into the letter A, the gate of non-arising.
The white tuft of hair is signless and perfectly all-knowing, Perfectly and eternally illuminating like the sun and moon.
The actions of body, speech, and mind constitute the three secrets; These three secrets are themselves the manifested and transformed dharmas.
The five wheels and five wisdoms are the five parts, And these five parts entirely encompass the wheel of the Dharma-realm.
Akṣobhya, Ratnasaṃbhava, the Savior of the World, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi— the King—
accomplish the auspicious wheel of siddhi and transmit this sublime Dharma to transform all beings.
Trilokavijaya, sovereign of loving-kindness, Vajrasattva, the Immovable Honored One—
having fulfilled your vows according to the appointed time, complete the yoga rites and return to the golden realm.
The Buddha said:
“The syllable *A* is the lord of the Vajra family and presides over the liver.

The syllable *A* is the Dharma-body of the principle of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata; it is the seed-syllable of the Vajra Earth-wheel, which is intrinsically pure, the ultimate principle, and ultimately ungraspable emptiness. It is the maṇḍala of the Vajra family.”

If we consider it in terms of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), earth is a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*). Among the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the consciousness aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*)—the mind—sustains the earth, and its seeds are impure.
Generally, the five viscera are material phenomena.

Among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) arises from the mind; in terms of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), earth is a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*).
Now, the liver governs the *hun* (soul); the spirit and vital energy of the *hun* correspond to the East and Wood, and Wood is the emptiness of form (*rūpa-śūnyatā*).

Wood presides over spring, and its color is green; the green color arises from wood, and wood arises from water. The liver arises from the green qi and the kidneys; its shape is like that of an upright lotus leaf, with a pearl-like mass situated in its center—the "pearl-flesh" located on the left side of the chest.
The liver issues forth as the eyes and governs the tendons; where the tendons terminate, they become the nails.
Now, because the five gates of letters govern the five viscera and six bowels, this is merely to clarify the intermingling of the internal and external.
Furthermore, sour flavors predominantly enter the liver; they increase the strength of the liver but damage the spleen.
If there is no *hun* (soul) within the spleen, one will frequently experience drowsiness and confusion. This harms the liver and brings about disease, just as metal overcomes wood.

When the lungs are strong and the liver is weak, one should fix the mind upon the lungs; by taking in white breath with blue breath, the liver disease will be cured, for the blue breath has taken hold.

The syllable *VAM* is the lord of the Lotus Family and presides over the lungs. The syllable *VAM* is the eleventh transformation of the syllable *BA*, and the syllable *VI* is the third transformation; these explain the meaning of the syllable *A*, which is the seed-syllable of the Great Wheel of the Ocean of Wisdom of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata.
The dharma of sovereign supernormal powers is called the Wisdom Dharmakāya, and it is also called the Saṃbhogakāya; this is precisely the maṇḍala of the Lotus Family.
The lungs preside over the *po* (soul), and the *po* is the physical form.
Its shape is like a flower; it presides over the nose and is the metal of the western direction.
Metal presides over autumn, and its color is white.
White arises from wind, and wind arises from the yang energy of earth.

Within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is sustained by the wind of the mind; the mind of perception arises from consciousness (*vijñāna*); the mind of consciousness arises from past formations (*saṃskāra*); past formations arise from ignorance (*avidyā*); ignorance arises from delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*); and delusive conceptualization, in turn, arises from delusive conceptualization—thus revolving through the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
The lungs arise from white qi and are generated by the spleen; pungent flavors enter the lungs most frequently, which increases lung function but damages the liver.
If there is no *po* (the soul-faculty) within the lungs, one suffers from terror and insanity.
When the mind harms the lungs, illness arises, just as fire overcomes metal.

If the mind is strong and the lungs are weak, one should restrain the mind within the mind; by means of white breath (*śveta-vāyu*), one gathers in the red breath (*rakta-vāyu*). Thus, the lung disease will be cured. "White breath" refers to the syllable *A*.
"The syllable *Lam* belongs to the Jewel Family (*Ratnakula*) and presides over the mind.

The syllable *Lam* is the seed-syllable of the fire element from the ground of the heart of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata; it is the dwelling place of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. It incinerates the dust and grime of beginningless ignorance and false attachments of all sentient beings, giving rise to the sprout of the bodhicitta. It further explains the meaning of the syllable *A*; that is to say, it is the Tathāgata of the Response and Transformation Bodies, and in reality, it is the Fire-Arising Maṇḍala of the Wisdom Dharmakāya."
The mind presides over the spirit; its form is like a bird, and it is the fire of the south.
Fire presides over summer, and its color is red.
Red arises from fire, and fire arises from wood.

Within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) holds fire within the mind; this sensation arises from the mind of perception (*saṃjñā-citta*), and the mind, in turn, arises from the red vapor and the liver.

From the mind, the tongue emerges, which presides over blood; when the blood reaches its limit, it becomes milk, and it also presides over the ears, transforming into the nose, throat, nasal bridge, forehead, chin, and so forth.
The bitter taste predominantly enters the heart; it increases [the strength of] the heart and diminishes the lungs.
If the heart lacks its spirit, one frequently forgets what precedes and follows.
When the kidneys harm the heart, disease is formed, just as water overcomes fire.

If the kidneys are strong and the heart is weak, one should cause the mind to rest upon the kidneys; by using the red qi to absorb the black qi, the disease of the heart will be cured. The "red qi" refers to the character [the syllable].

“The syllable *Haṃ* belongs to the Karma family and presides over the kidneys. The syllable *Hūṃ* is a transformation of the syllable *Ha*; it is the seed-syllable of the wind element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*) for the eternally abiding lifespan of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata. It signifies the meaning of the three gates of liberation and the non-apprehensibility of the three time periods; it is the maṇḍala of the great power of the Dharmakāya.”
Wind is that which is sustained by the mind within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
As for the five viscera, they are the liver, lungs, heart, spleen, and kidneys.
The stomach is another name for one of the six hollow organs (*ṣaḍ-koṣṭhaka*).
The stomach is this abdomen; grain is the visceral receptacle of the spleen.

It is the sea for the five solid organs and six hollow viscera. All water and grain enter the stomach; the five solid organs and six hollow viscera all receive their sustenance from the stomach. Each of the five flavors flows separately, yet it is the refined and bland flavor that enters the stomach; thus, the kidneys receive their nourishment from the stomach.
The kidneys are located below the navel and the waist; the one on the left is called the kidney (*shen*), and the one on the right is called the gate of life (*mingmen*).
The kidneys spread throughout the heart, abdomen, and stomach; they are the kidneys that receive and discharge the essence of water.
The kidneys govern the will (*zhi*) and correspond to the north and water.

Water presides over winter; its color is black. Among the five *yin* elements, the *xing-yin* (active-yin) mind holds water. The active-mind arises from the receiving-mind (*shou-xin*), and the receiving-mind arises from the perceiving-mind (*xiang*). The kidneys arise from black qi and the lungs, and they govern the ears.
The kidneys emerge as the bones and govern the marrow; when the marrow reaches its limit, it forms the ears and breasts, and when the bones reach their limit, they form the teeth.
An excess of the salty flavor enters the kidneys, strengthening them while weakening the heart.
If there is no willpower within the kidneys, one weeps and wails excessively.
When the spleen harms the kidneys, it forms a disease, like earth overcoming water.
If the spleen is strong and the kidneys are weak, one should fix the mind upon the spleen; by using black qi to draw in yellow qi, the kidney disease will be cured.
The black qi is the seed-syllable.
The syllable *khaṃ* belongs to the Space Family (*ākāśa-kula*) and governs the spleen.

This syllable *khaṃ* is the Great Emptiness Wisdom (*mahā-śūnyatā-jñāna*), the locus of quiescent True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the wisdom of principle realized by the Five Buddhas through the Unseen Uṣṇīṣa of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata; it is the supreme maṇḍala of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) realized by all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time.
The spleen is associated with intention (*manas*), and constitutes the center and the element of earth (*pṛthivī*).
Earth presides over the late summer, and its color is yellow.

Yellow arises from earth, and earth arises from fire, as previously explained regarding how, among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)—the mind—sustains earth.
Alternatively, it may serve as the wood-vessel; the green of the wood is emptiness.
The spleen arises from the yellow qi and from the heart; it governs the mouth and constitutes the will (*chih*).
Sweet flavors enter the spleen most readily; they increase the spleen but damage the kidneys.
If there is no intention within the spleen, it will become greatly confused.
If the liver harms the spleen, it forms a disease, like wood overcoming earth.
When the liver is strong and the spleen is weak, one should fix the mind upon the liver, using yellow qi to absorb the blue qi; thus, the spleen disease will be cured.
The yellow qi is the "character" (zi); the five viscera are like lotus flowers drooping downward.
"Internally the five viscera, externally the five phases, emerging to form the physical body"—this is the "name" (ming).

Form (*rūpa*) consists of the four great elements and the five sense faculties; name (*nāman*) refers to the mind and the other four aggregates, such as perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*).
These constitute the sun, the moon, the five planets, the twelve lunar mansions, and the twenty-eight constellations, which form the body of a human being.
Mountains, seas, and the great earth emerge from the syllable A;
rivers and streams emerge from the syllable Vaṃ;
gold, jewels, precious gems, the sun and moon, the stars, and the radiance of fire-pearls are formed from the syllable Laṃ.
The five grains, fruits, and various flowers bloom because they are formed by the inclusion of the syllable *haṃ*.
Fragrances, beautiful forms, the nourishment of the colors and flavors of humans and devas, as well as upright features, merit, and nobility, are adorned by the syllable *aṃ*.

The syllable *A* is the Tathāgata Akṣobhya of the east; the syllable *Vaṃ* is the Tathāgata Amitābha of the west; the syllable *Raṃ* is the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava of the south; and the syllable *Haṃ* is the Great Sun Tathāgata Vairocana.

The meaning of the letter A is the profoundly deep, empty, and quiescent essence; it cannot be grasped, nor can it be relinquished. This is the Mother of Dharmas, the Great Empowerment of the letter A.

The syllable *A* is a teaching difficult to believe; let those of the Hīnayāna and the Vinaya masters especially not see it. This original Sanskrit manuscript of the five sections consists of four hundred thousand words, extracted from the *Vairocana Sūtra* and the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*. Having gathered the essential and subtle points, this supreme field of merit consists solely of these five-syllable mantras.
The merit obtained by the reciter is incomparable, inconceivable, and ineffable.

By receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and contemplating the rational nature of the mantras of the five families of the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, one causes oneself to obtain blessings: the bones become firm, the body robust, and one is forever free from calamities, obstacles, and all suffering of illness, thereby being sustained in long life.

These five syllable-gates are the crest-jewels of the five wisdoms and the very heart of the five Buddhas; they are the mother of the quiescent wisdom of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, the nurturing parents of all sentient beings, and the treasury of the dharma-realm throughout the ten directions.

Because it enables one to wage war against the evil Māras of the three periods of time and achieve victory over them throughout the three periods—serving as armor, helmets, spears, shields, bows, arrows, and weapons—the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time enter into this and are born from within it.
The tooth is the seed-syllable.
Furthermore, regarding this yoga seat: the square wheel of golden vajra is itself the Vajrāsana.
*Ā*, O Vajrabhūmi! Contemplate the syllable *Ā* as the earth and as the Vajrāsana.
VAṂ: the Vajra Water Family; one should visualize two VAṂ syllables as water and lotus flowers.
LAṂ: the Vajra Fire Family; one should visualize three LAṂ syllables as the sun.
Haṃ: the Vajra-Wind Family; visualize the fourth syllable, Haṃ, as the moon.
Khaṃ: the Vajra-Space Family; visualize the fifth syllable, Khaṃ, as space.
This is the contemplation on the unborn nature of the Tathāgata.
These five sections of mantras are the precious nectar of non-arising for all Tathāgatas, the wondrous medicine of the *tīrthika* (supreme) Buddha-nature.

If even a single character enters the five viscera, ten thousand ailments will not arise; how much more so when practicing the contemplation of the sun and the contemplation of the moon—one shall immediately realize the empty stillness of the Buddha-body.

A, VAṂ, RAṂ, HAṂ, KHAṂ—these five characters above are the Dharma-body mantras. If one recites them once, seven times, twenty-one times, or forty-nine times each day, the merit compared is such that the blessing of a single recitation is equal to reciting the entire Tripitaka one million times; this includes all the scriptures. How much more so for one who, in meditative stillness, enters the gate of samādhi and contemplates the letter A with clear and discerning precision, like the sun shining upon the sky—this is the direct observation of Buddha-nature, and the merit obtained therein is beyond measure.

The phrases of this secret treasury are truly inconceivable; I only fear that the Dharma-preachers among the śrāvakas and those who uphold the Vinaya of the Hīnayāna will give rise to doubt and fail to believe, which would instead increase their transgressions.

For example, suppose a king has a young son whom he especially cherishes; he would exhaust his treasury and storehouses of precious jewels without regret, yet he would not give him the swords Ganjiang and Moye, fearing that the boy might not know how to use them and would thereby injure his body.
For this reason, the Tathāgata secretly transmits [this teaching] to the great bodhisattvas and does not grant it to those of inferior wisdom, such as the śrāvakas.
Dharmatātathatā: the Dharmakāya Tathāgata is the ultimate reality.

From the armpits to the crown of the head is the superior; from the navel to the armpits is the middling; and from the feet to the navel is the inferior. Within the mantras, one should accordingly distinguish these three types of accomplishment.

The lower grade of *siddhi*: A-ra-pa-ca-na; this is called the "Emergent *Siddhi*. It is able to produce roots and stems that pervade the four directions. Reciting it once is equivalent to reciting the Tripitaka one hundred times; reciting it once is equivalent to reciting the eighty-four thousand *Veda* collections. It eliminates all hardships and difficulties for the practitioner, immediately entering the equality of all dharmas of the Tathāgata. All syllables are likewise equal, and one swiftly attains the accomplishment of *Mahāprajñā*.

Reciting this twice eliminates the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over billions of kalpas; Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra follow behind, the fourfold assembly surrounds them as if on guard, and the benevolent, fearless Dharma-protecting spirits stand before that person.

If one recites it three times, samādhi will manifest before them; if one recites it four times, they will possess total retention without forgetting; if one recites it five times, they will swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
The middling siddhi:

A, Vī, RA, HŪṂ, KHAṂ—these are called the entry into siddhi. They are able to produce branches and leaves that fill the four directions; their radiance shines forth as they enter the Buddha-dharmadhātu, and this is called entry into siddhi.

If one recites this once, it is equivalent to reciting the Tripitaka one thousand times; this is called the adamantine syllables that subdue the four māras and the six realms of existence, and fulfill the wisdom of all-knowledge.
The supreme siddhi:
A, Vaṃ, Raṃ, Haṃ, Khaṃ. These are called the secret siddhi, also called the accomplishment siddhi, and also called the su-siddhi; su-siddhi is the pervasion of the dharma-realm.

Accomplishing the fruit of Buddhahood and realizing great bodhi, the light of the dharmadhātu’s secret mantra pervades everywhere; only Buddhas and Buddhas can enter this gate, while pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas cannot illuminate it—this is also called the secret siddhi.
If one recites it once, it is equivalent to turning the Tripitaka one million times.
The *siddhi* of emergence extends from the feet to the waist; the *siddhi* of entry extends from the navel to the heart; and the secret *siddhi* extends from the heart to the crown of the head.

These three types of *siddhi* are as follows: the emergence of *siddhi* is the accomplishment of the *nirmāṇakāya*; the entry into *siddhi* is the accomplishment of the *saṃbhogakāya*; and the secret *siddhi*, the *susiddhi*, is the accomplishment of the *dharmakāya*. In truth, these are the three eternal bodies, the treasury of the True Dharma.

The Dharmakāya Vairocana is the embodiment of perfection, the true source of the five families and the three families; therefore, I prostrate and pay homage to Buddha Vairocana. These five characters are the fifteen characters; they are the fifteen kinds of vajra-samādhi.

One character is the fifteen characters, and the fifteen characters are one character. One character is the five characters, and the five characters are one character. Rotating in both reverse and direct order, beginning and end are non-dual.

Now, within these eight gates, all phenomena are subsumed: a single character subsumes all characters, and all characters subsume a single character; one explains all characters by means of a single character, and one explains a single character by means of all characters; one establishes all characters by means of a single character, and one establishes a single character by means of all characters; one refutes all characters by means of a single character, and one refutes a single character by means of all characters. This meaning consists of one forward recitation and one reverse recitation, followed by four rotations in the forward direction and four rotations in the reverse direction; it is the principle that benefits all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, causing them all to attain Buddhahood.

The *svedasthāna-citta* (the heart of ordinary beings) is here translated as the "heart of reality. Its form is like that of a lotus bud closed but not yet opened; it is bound by sinews and veins to form eight divisions. In men, it points upward; in women, it points downward.
Contemplate this lotus so that it blossoms into an eight-petaled white lotus. Upon its pedestal, contemplate the syllable *A*, which is the color of a vajra.

Furthermore, the syllable *A* is like a square yellow altar, and one’s body is situated within it. From the syllable *A*, the syllable *Ra* emerges; once the body has been incinerated and entirely reduced to ashes, from within these ashes arises the syllable *Ba*, which is pure white in color. From this, the five wheel-syllables—*A*, *Vaṃ*, *Rāṃ*, *Haṃ*, and *Khaṃ*—are produced, and they are immediately established in the five locations of the body, from the waist down to the crown of the head; these are called the "purified bodhicitta."
Taking these five syllable-gates as the condition for generating the root of great compassion, the Buddha—the King of Śāla Trees—grows and spreads, filling the entire dharma-realm.
Yet all dharmas, by means of these very five syllable-gates, are fundamentally unarisen, beyond verbal expression, pure by nature, devoid of causes and conditions, and like empty space.

This constitutes the eight-petaled stage. From the navel to the heart is the vajra pedestal; the stalk stands in the midst of the ocean, with the navel serving as the great sea. From the navel downward are the positions of the deities who dwell on this earth, situated along the shore of the ocean.
This means that from the ocean of the great compassion of all Buddhas, Vajra-wisdom is born; from Vajra-wisdom, all Buddha-assemblies are produced.

Upon this heart-lotus with its eight petals, one contemplates the letter *A*. From this letter, immeasurable light radiates forth, dispersing from the heart and coalescing into a garland of light, like a floral wreath, pervading all Buddha-fields. This light encircles the practitioner’s body from the crown of the head down to the feet.

Furthermore, one contemplates the syllable *Aṃ* at the crown of the head, which transforms into the Central Womb (*garbha*) Mandala. From this syllable, three layers of radiant flames arise: the first layer of light encircles the area above the throat, extending from the throat to the crown of the head;

wherever it reaches, the various deities appear accordingly, forming the first court mandala. Next, the second layer of light encircles the heart; from the navel upward to the throat, the various deities appear accordingly, forming the second-layer mandala.

Next, the third layer of light encircles the area above the navel; from the navel downward, the various deities appear accordingly, forming the third-layer mandala, which is the Court of Worldly Devas (*laukika-deva-kula*).

The forms, colors, and marks of the various honored ones are each distinct and fully present within one’s own body, as if personally entering the Buddha’s assembly; thus, one’s own body becomes the entire maṇḍala-body, which is precisely the body of the universal Dharma-realm.
The "womb" (*garbha*) therein is the eight-petaled lotus of Vairocana’s own mind.
Upon this lotus throne of the mind, it serves as the central womb of the maṇḍala; the eight petals outside it are likewise arranged according to the positions of the Buddhas.
The four cardinal directions are the four wisdoms of the Tathāgata, and the petals at the four corners are the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Furthermore, Samantabhadra in the southeast is the bodhicitta; this is the wondrous cause.
Next, Mañjuśrī in the southwest represents great wisdom.
Next, Maitreya in the northeast represents great compassion.
Both great compassion and great mercy constitute the second meaning.
Next, the Avalokiteśvara in the northwest represents realization; that is to say, through the fulfillment of practice and vows, one enters this samādhi of the lotus pedestal.
Within the petals of the four directions, the initial letter *A* is located in the east, symbolizing the bodhicitta, which is the very beginning of the myriad practices.
Yellow is the vajra-nature; its name is Ratnaketu, and it is also named Akṣobhya Buddha.

Next, the syllable *A* in the south represents practice (*caryā*); it is red in color, signifying fire, which is identical in meaning to Mañjuśrī. It is the blossoming of flowers, and is also named Ratnasambhava Buddha.

Next, the syllable *Aṃ* is in the western direction; it is bodhi. Because of the myriad practices, one achieves equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Its white color signifies the ultimate meaning of perfect luminosity, and it also carries the meaning of water. That Buddha is named Amitābha.

Next, the character "Evil" (Ē) is located in the north; it is the fruit of Perfect Enlightenment. The Buddha there is named Dundubhisvara, who is Śākyamuni himself. This is precisely Great Nirvāṇa; because his traces have reached their ultimate limit and returned to the source, it is called Nirvāṇa.
Because the Sun of the Buddha has already set behind the mountain of Nirvana, its color is black.

Next, one enters into the center; the syllables *e*, *laṃ*, and *śva* are the skillful means by which one realizes that the essence of this mind, the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), is from the beginning a state of eternal quiescence. This is the body of Vairocana’s original ground, the substance of the lotus pedestal, transcending the eight petals and devoid of spatial location; it is not a realm of the conceptual mind, known only by Buddhas and Buddhas.
By this skillful means, they are identical to the Great Emptiness while manifesting all forms; the center is empty yet possesses all colors, which is the empowerment of the world.

The assembly of the Universal Gate of the Maṇḍala exists everywhere; however, it is but the single body, single wisdom, and single practice of the Tathāgata. Therefore, the eight petals are all the one essence of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata.

Therefore, the Honored One of the Center, the Great Sun, is the Dharmakāya; the Lord of Secrets with the Vajra Wisdom Seal is Prajñā; and Avalokiteśvara holding the Lotus Seal is Vimukti. Thus, the Body Secret is the virtue of the Dharmakāya, the Speech Secret is the virtue of Prajñā, and the Mind Secret is the virtue of Vimukti.

Through *prajñā* one attains liberation, and liberation is caused by *prajñā*; these two rely upon the essence of the *dharmakāya*, being neither identical nor separate, for if either were missing, they could not exist—just like the three dots of the letter *i*. Bodhicitta is this Vajra family; Great Compassion is the Lotus family; and skillful means is the Nirmāṇakāya.
Therefore, the syllable *A* is within the womb, indicating the stage prior to Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*);
the syllable *Sa* is outside the womb, indicating the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*vimalabodhi*);
and the syllable *Va* is the function, whereby all dharmas revolve in reliance upon this gate, manifesting the two types of transformation at will to deliver beings throughout the ten realms.

This seal of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is the true mark of the mind and the fruit of the knowledge of all-knowledge; it takes the bodhicitta as its cause, great compassion as its root, and skillful means as its culmination, with the fivefold meanings of the gateways to all-knowledge serving as its manifold conditions.

If there are sentient beings who understand this teaching, people of the world should make offerings to them as they would revere a *caitya*. A *caitya* is that upon which the bodily relics (*śarīra*) rely; therefore, all gods and people of the world who seek blessings and protection make offerings to it.
If a practitioner accepts and upholds this meaning, it is the locus of the *dharmakāya* relics.
Furthermore, since the Sanskrit terms *caitya* and *citta* share the same essential nature, the secret significance herein is that the mind itself is the Buddha-stūpa.

Just as in the third maṇḍala, which takes the self-mind as its foundation and gradually increases in layers up to the central womb (*garbha*), with the color of nirvāṇa situated at its very summit, this caitya is therefore exceedingly high.

Furthermore, from the central womb, it increases sequentially through the eight petals until, in the third stage, the Universal Gate Body (Pumen-shen) pervades everywhere according to the various types of beings; therefore, this caitya is exceedingly vast.
The *dharmadhātu* of the lotus pedestal is what is called the *śarīra* of the Dharma-body.
If sentient beings understand this seal of the Bodhicitta-mind, they are identical to Vairocana; therefore it is said:
"The world should make offerings to them, just as one honors a *caitya*."

However, the body and land of Vairocana are mutually integrated as the environment and its inhabitants, and their nature and characteristics are identical. True Suchness pervades the entire Dharma-realm as the Great Self; his body, speech, and mind are equal to the great void, taking space as his site of practice and the Dharma-realm as his couch.
The Tathāgata Mahāvairocana, in order to cause beings to know and see this path, manifests two kinds of *dharmakāya*:

the Wisdom *Dharmakāya* Buddha abides in the principle of *bhūtalakṣaṇa* (the true nature of phenomena) for his own enjoyment, manifesting thirty-seven honored ones to lead all beings into the path of non-duality;

the Principle *Dharmakāya* Buddha abides in the dharma of suchness-quiet illumination, yet remains eternally unmoving while manifesting upon the eight-petaled [lotus] for the enjoyment of both himself and others, displaying the threefold maṇḍala to enable the ten realms to realize the Great Void.

Although there are distinctions between principle and wisdom and differences in their breadth or brevity, they have from the beginning been a single dharma, never differing at all; all phenomena return to the single letter *A*, and the five families are one with Vairocana.
Relying upon the Buddha Vairocana, I open the heart-seal of wisdom to establish this foundational meaning;
adorned universally with immeasurable merit, may I enter together with all the Sugatas into the dhāraṇī.
May those practitioners who share this affinity dwell securely in the unsurpassed ocean of purity.
One fascicle of the Secret Mantra Method for the Threefold Siddhi.
